claim: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is found worldwide with high immunoglobulin G (IgG) sero-prevalence rates of 56–94% depending on the respective countries.
source: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) constitutes the prototypical human pathogenic β-herpesvirus found worldwide with high immunoglobulin G (IgG) sero-prevalence rates of 56–94% depending on the respective countries (Zuhair et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zuhair et al., 2019.

claim: HCMV encodes the largest known transcriptome of human viruses.
source: HCMV encodes the largest known transcriptome of human viruses (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012.

claim: HCMV encodes a huge and varied arsenal of immunoevasins that counteract immune recognition of infected cells facilitating virus persistence, shedding, and superinfection of sero-positive hosts.
source: HCMV encodes the largest known transcriptome of human viruses (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012), giving rise to an equally large antigenic proteome including a huge and varied arsenal of immunoevasins (Berry et al., 2020; Hengel et al., 1998) that counteract immune recognition of infected cells facilitating virus persistence, shedding, and superinfection of sero-positive hosts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2020 and Hengel et al., 1998.

claim: Concentrated HCMV-immune IgG preparations (e.g. Cytotect) are used to prevent infection of immunocompromised patients including the prevention of congenital infection in primary infected pregnant women with varying degrees of success.
source: Besides antiviral therapy involving nucleotide analogs, concentrated HCMV-immune IgG preparations (e.g. Cytotect) are used to prevent infection of immunocompromised patients including the prevention of congenital infection in primary infected pregnant women with varying degrees of success (Kagan et al., 2019; Revello et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kagan et al., 2019 and Revello et al., 2014.

claim: Clinical isolates of HCMV tend to disseminate via cell-to-cell spread, thus avoiding an encounter with neutralizing antibodies.
source: Generally, HCMV is observed to withstand a humoral immunity even replicating and disseminating in the presence of highly neutralizing immune sera in vitro and clinical isolates of HCMV tend to disseminate via cell-to-cell spread, thus avoiding an encounter with neutralizing antibodies (Falk et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Falk et al., 2018.

claim: HCMV encodes a set of Fcγ-binding glycoproteins (viral FcγRs, vFcγRs) that have been shown to antagonize host FcγR activation by immune IgG.
source: Notably, HCMV encodes a set of Fcγ-binding glycoproteins (viral FcγRs, vFcγRs) that have been shown to antagonize host FcγR activation by immune IgG (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b.

claim: HCMV gp34, gp68 and HSV-1 gE/gI efficiently antagonize the activation of human FcγRs.
source: In this previous study, we showed that HCMV gp34, gp68 and HSV-1 gE/gI efficiently antagonize the activation of human FcγRs.
evidence: The claim refers to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Fcγ mediated immune control is essential not only for the effectiveness of non-neutralizing but also neutralizing IgG antibodies.
source: As it has become increasingly evident that Fcγ mediated immune control is essential not only for the effectiveness of non-neutralizing but also neutralizing IgG antibodies (DiLillo et al., 2014; Forthal et al., 2013; Horwitz et al., 2017; Van den Hoecke et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DiLillo et al., 2014; Forthal et al., 2013; Horwitz et al., 2017; Van den Hoecke et al., 2017.

claim: HCMV is the only virus known so far that encodes more than one individual molecule with the capacity to bind Fcγ.
source: While several herpesviruses encode vFcγRs, HCMV is the only virus known so far that encodes more than one individual molecule with the capacity to bind Fcγ.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: HCMV encodes four distinct molecules which share the ability to bind Fcγ: gp68 (UL119-118), gp34 (RL11), gp95 (RL12), and gpRL13 (RL13).
source: Specifically, HCMV encodes four distinct molecules which share this ability: gp68 (UL119-118), gp34 (RL11), gp95 (RL12), and gpRL13 (RL13) (Atalay et al., 2002; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014a; Cortese et al., 2012; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Atalay et al., 2002; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014a; Cortese et al., 2012; Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: Mouse CMV (MCMV) encoded m138 has been shown to bind Fcγ.
source: Turning to other species, mouse CMV (MCMV) encoded m138 has been shown to bind Fcγ, yet it has more prominently been associated with a variety of unrelated functions proving m138 not to be a strict homolog of the HCMV counterparts (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arapović et al., 2009 and Lenac et al., 2006.

claim: Rhesus CMV (RhCMV) encodes an Fcγ-binding protein in the Rh05 gene (RL11 gene family).
source: We recently found Rhesus CMV (RhCMV) to encode an Fcγ-binding protein in the Rh05 gene (RL11 gene family) seemingly more closely related to its HCMV analog (Kolb et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kolb et al., 2019.

claim: gpRh05 is able to generically antagonize activation of all macaque FcγRs.
source: This is supported by the fact that gpRh05, as HCMV vFcγRs gp34 and gp68, is able to generically antagonize activation of all macaque FcγRs.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: gp68 and gp34 are able to engage in antibody bipolar bridging (ABB) forming ternary complexes consisting of antigen, antibody, and vFcγR.
source: In recent years it has been shown that gp68 and gp34 are able to engage in antibody bipolar bridging (ABB) forming ternary complexes consisting of antigen, antibody, and vFcγR (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014a; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014a; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b; Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: gp68 has been shown to bind IgG in a 2:1 ratio.
source: Moreover, gp68 has been shown to bind IgG in a 2:1 ratio and has the ability to internalize and translocate IgG to lysosomal compartments, while gp34 has been shown to form predominantly homo-dimeric structures (Ndjamen et al., 2016; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ndjamen et al., 2016 and Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: gp68 has the ability to internalize and translocate IgG to lysosomal compartments.
source: Moreover, gp68 has been shown to bind IgG in a 2:1 ratio and has the ability to internalize and translocate IgG to lysosomal compartments, while gp34 has been shown to form predominantly homo-dimeric structures (Ndjamen et al., 2016; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ndjamen et al., 2016 and Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: gp34 has been shown to form predominantly homo-dimeric structures.
source: Moreover, gp68 has been shown to bind IgG in a 2:1 ratio and has the ability to internalize and translocate IgG to lysosomal compartments, while gp34 has been shown to form predominantly homo-dimeric structures (Ndjamen et al., 2016; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ndjamen et al., 2016 and Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: gp68 binding to IgG has been mapped to the CH2–CH3 interdomain region of Fcγ.
source: gp68 binding to IgG has been mapped to the CH2–CH3 interdomain region of Fcγ (Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: gp68 was only able to bind wtFc but not nbFc.
source: Expectedly, gp68 was only able to bind wtFc but not nbFc whereas gp34, comparable to human FcγRI, retained binding to both wtFc and nbFc (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: gp34, comparable to human FcγRI, retained binding to both wtFc and nbFc.
source: Expectedly, gp68 was only able to bind wtFc but not nbFc whereas gp34, comparable to human FcγRI, retained binding to both wtFc and nbFc (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FcγRIIA exhibited reduced binding to nbFc.
source: Consequently, FcγRII exhibited reduced binding to nbFc (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: gp34 binding involves the hinge region of monomeric IgG.
source: Since gp34 showed intact binding similar to host FcγRI but not FcγRIIA we surmised that gp34 binding involves the hinge region of monomeric IgG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: PGS-precipitation of FcγRI/CD64, exclusively recognizing the hinge region on IgG, was almost abrogated by the LALA mutations.
source: PGS-precipitation of FcγRI/CD64, exclusively recognizing the hinge region on IgG, was almost abrogated by the mutations in the LALA variant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: gp34 was sensitive to the LALA mutations, albeit to a lower extent than FcγRI/CD64.
source: Similarly, gp34 was sensitive to the mutations, albeit to a lower extent than FcγRI/CD64.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The interaction of gp68 with B12 was unaffected by the LALA point mutations.
source: As expected, the interaction of gp68 with B12 was unaffected by the LALA point mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: When precipitating His-tagged sgp68 in the presence of monomeric IgG, co-precipitation of sgp34 but no co-precipitation of sgp34mtrp was observed.
source: When precipitating His-tagged sgp68 in the presence of monomeric IgG, we observed co-precipitation of sgp34 but no co-precipitation of sgp34mtrp (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dose-dependent binding of sgp68 to titrated amounts of immobilized sgp34 was observed.
source: Here, we observed dose-dependent binding of sgp68 to titrated amounts of immobilized sgp34.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: sgp68 could only be detected in the presence of IgG1 but not IgA.
source: sgp68 could only be detected in the presence of IgG1 but not IgA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: sgp68 binding in the presence of IgG1 and sgp34mtrp does not exceed background levels.
source: Furthermore, sgp68 binding in the presence of IgG1 and sgp34mtrp in this setup does not exceed background levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: gp34 and gp68 are able to simultaneously bind to IgG with gp34 binding to the upper hinge region and gp68 binding to the CH2–CH3 interface domain on IgG.
source: Taken together, we conclude that gp34 and gp68 are able to simultaneously bind to IgG with gp34 binding to the upper hinge region and gp68 binding to the CH2–CH3 interface domain on IgG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: FcγRIIIA activation is antagonized efficiently by a virus co-expressing both gp34 and gp68.
source: In line with previously published observations (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b) we found that FcγRIIIA activation is antagonized efficiently by a virus co-expressing both gp34 and gp68 while viruses expressing either gp34 or gp68 show only minor or no antagonistic potential when compared with a mutant lacking all vFcγRs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b.

claim: Viruses expressing either gp34 or gp68 show only minor or no antagonistic potential when compared with a mutant lacking all vFcγRs.
source: In line with previously published observations (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b) we found that FcγRIIIA activation is antagonized efficiently by a virus co-expressing both gp34 and gp68 while viruses expressing either gp34 or gp68 show only minor or no antagonistic potential when compared with a mutant lacking all vFcγRs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Primary NK cell activation in response to target cells decorated with anti-HCMV antibodies was antagonized by a virus expressing both gp34 and gp68 with high significance.
source: In line with the reporter cell assay, primary NK cell activation in response to target cells decorated with anti-HCMV antibodies was antagonized by a virus expressing both gp34 and gp68 with high significance, while the mutant viruses lacking gp34 or gp68 showed drastically lower antagonistic potential (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutant viruses lacking gp34 or gp68 showed drastically lower antagonistic potential in NK cell activation.
source: In line with the reporter cell assay, primary NK cell activation in response to target cells decorated with anti-HCMV antibodies was antagonized by a virus expressing both gp34 and gp68 with high significance, while the mutant viruses lacking gp34 or gp68 showed drastically lower antagonistic potential (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: gp34 and gp68 antagonize FcγRs by synergizing modes of action.
source: From these observations we conclude that gp34 and gp68 antagonize FcγRs by synergizing modes of action, suggesting cooperation, at least in the absence of gp95 (RL12) and gpRL13 (RL13).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The cytosolic tail of gp68 harbors an YXXΦ motif seven aa downstream of the transmembrane domain.
source: The cytosolic tail of gp68 harbors an YXXΦ motif seven aa downstream of the transmembrane domain.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis described in the text.

claim: The YXXΦ motif has been described as a marker for lysosomal targeting.
source: Such a motif has been described as a marker for lysosomal targeting (Bonifacino and Traub, 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bonifacino and Traub, 2003.

claim: The cytosolic tail of gp34 encodes a di-leucine [D/E]XXX[LL/LI] motif which is unique among surface-resident vFcγRs.
source: Conversely, the cytosolic tail of gp34 encodes a di-leucine [D/E]XXX[LL/LI] motif which we find to be unique among surface-resident vFcγRs.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis described in the text.

claim: Upon recombinant expression, surface exposition of Fcγ binding gp68 is drastically increased when CD4-tailed although overall protein expression was comparable.
source: This revealed that upon recombinant expression, surface exposition of Fcγ binding gp68 is drastically increased when CD4-tailed although overall protein expression was comparable and all constructs bear original signal peptides (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Internalization of complete IC was drastically reduced with CD4-tailed gp68.
source: This can be attributed to the abrogation of its internalization evidenced by the fact that internalization of complete IC was drastically reduced with CD4-tailed gp68 when tracking hCD20/Rtx ICs using pulse-chase flow cytometry (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: gp34 proved to rapidly internalize complete Rtx-CD20 IC only with its native cytosolic tail intact.
source: Conversely, while gp34 showed only mild differences in surface exposition when altered in the same way (Figure 3C), it proved to rapidly internalize complete Rtx-CD20 IC only with its native cytosolic tail intact (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: gp34 more efficiently internalizes even non-immune IgG compared to gp68.
source: Further, while we also observe gp34 to more efficiently internalize even non-immune IgG, the still rapid internalization of non-immune IgG by gp68 seems not to translate to the internalization of IC regarding efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A major task of gp34 compared to gp68 is mediating the efficient internalization of IC.
source: As we observed significantly more efficient internalization of IC by gp34wt compared to gp68wt or HSV-1 gEwt (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we conclude that a major task of gp34 compared to gp68 is mediating the efficient internalization of IC, a feature likely linked to its particular di-leucine cytosolic motif.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the context of HCMV infection gp68 is more surface resident compared to gp34.
source: As previously reported (Atalay et al., 2002; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b) and confirmed in this study, we find that in the context of HCMV infection gp68 is more surface resident compared to gp34 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Atalay et al., 2002 and Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b.

claim: gp68 but not gp34 significantly reduces binding of FcγRIIIA to cell surface immune complexes compared to CD99.
source: We found gp68 but not gp34 to significantly reduce binding of FcγRIIIA to cell surface immune complexes compared to CD99 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FcγRI is not blocked by gp68 or gp34.
source: Finally, this conclusion is further substantiated by our observation that FcγRI, which binds to IgG independently of the above-mentioned residues in the CH2–CH3 interdomain region (Shields et al., 2001), is not blocked by gp68 or gp34 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Shields et al., 2001.

claim: FcγRIII binding to opsonized HCMV-infected cells is strongly reduced in the presence of gp68, but not gp34.
source: Evaluating the results from three independent experiments performed with independent virus preparations confirmed a strong relative reduction in FcγRIIIA binding to opsonized HCMV-infected cells in the presence of gp68, but not gp34 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: gp68 shows an approximate 60% reduction in FcγRIII binding.
source: This finding is in line with our previous gain-of-function experiments (Figure 4C) again showing an approximate 60% reduction in FcγRIII binding.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data described in the text.

claim: Binding of FcγRI was only slightly reduced in the presence of either vFcγR, but clearly reduced in the presence of both molecules.
source: While not further elaborated on in this study, we also measured binding of FcγRs I, IIA, and IIB/C in the same setup and observed that binding of FcγRI was only slightly reduced in the presence of either vFcγR, but clearly reduced in the presence of both molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: gp68 showed a similar effect on FcγRs IIA and IIB/C as observed for FcγRIII.
source: Conversely, gp68 showed a similar effect on FcγRs IIA and IIB/C as observed for FcγRIII (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: gp68 or gp34 individually confirmed to antagonize FcγRIII activation in the absence of non-immune IgG.
source: Using this approach, gp68 or gp34 individually confirmed to antagonize FcγRIII activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The more membrane resident gp68-CD4 showed a markedly stronger antagonistic effect compared to gp68wt.
source: However, the more membrane resident gp68-CD4 showed a markedly stronger antagonistic effect compared to gp68wt, indicating a more prominent membrane-residence of gp68 to be beneficial regarding evasion from FcγR recognition despite its lower capacity to internalize ICs (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When comparing unaltered gp34 to its less internalized gp34-CD4 variant an opposite effect was observed indicating internalization to be a major condition of gp34 driven antagonization of FcγR activation.
source: Conversely, when comparing unaltered gp34 to its less internalized gp34-CD4 variant we observed an opposite effect indicating internalization to be a major condition of gp34 driven antagonization of FcγR activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The presence of an excess of non-immune IgG interferes with both gp68 and gp34 antagonization in a dose-dependent manner.
source: This showed that indeed the presence of an excess of non-immune IgG interferes with both gp68 and gp34 antagonization in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: Synergism between gp34 and gp68 was optimal at a 100:1 ratio of non-immune Ifx over Hc.
source: Synergism between gp34 and gp68 was optimal at a 100:1 ratio of non-immune Ifx over Hc (Figure 6B, right panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: vFcγRs are particularly adapted to work in the presence of excess non-immune IgG.
source: Synergism between gp34 and gp68 was optimal at a 100:1 ratio of non-immune Ifx over Hc (Figure 6B, right panel) indicating that vFcγRs are particularly adapted to work in the presence of excess non-immune IgG, supporting our previous observation with human hyperimmunoglobulin Cytotect (see Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Natively expressed gp34 as well as gp68 are able to antagonize FcγRIIIA activation individually.
source: Although not statistically significant, this approach clearly demonstrated that compared to our observations with hyperimmunoglobulin Cytotect (see Figure 2), natively expressed gp34 as well as gp68 are able to antagonize FcγRIIIA activation individually.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: When both vFcγRs were expressed by HCMV-infected cells, a markedly stronger antagonistic effect was seen (p=0.0252).
source: When both vFcγRs were expressed by HCMV-infected cells, a markedly stronger antagonistic effect was seen (p=0.0252).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The ectodomain of gp68 is sufficient to enhance the antagonistic effect of gp34.
source: Here we observe that the ectodomain of gp68 is sufficient to enhance the antagonistic effect of gp34 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: gp34 is designed for internalization of IC while gp68 blocks FcγR binding to IC.
source: In summary, we conclude that (i) gp34 is designed for internalization of IC while gp68 blocks FcγR binding to IC
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: gp34 and gp68 are able to antagonize FcγR activation individually when faced with titrated amounts of immune IgG, but non-immune IgG interferes with this inhibition.
source: (ii) gp34 and gp68 are able to antagonize FcγR activation individually when faced with titrated amounts of immune IgG, but non-immune IgG interferes with this inhibition
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: gp34 and gp68 show cooperativity in attenuating FcγR activation particularly under conditions of high excess of non-immune IgG.
source: (iii) gp34 and gp68 show cooperativity in attenuating FcγR activation particularly under conditions of high excess of non-immune IgG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: gp34 and gp68 work in cooperation to achieve efficient antagonization of antibody-mediated effector mechanisms.
source: Supported by functional evaluation, we propose a model in which g34 and gp68 work in cooperation to achieve efficient antagonization of antibody-mediated effector mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: gp34 and gp68 actually depend on one another to efficiently antagonize NK cell degranulation.
source: However, when carefully examining their effect in a loss-of-function approach based on opsonized cells infected with a complete set of targeted HCMV gene deletion mutants, we convinced ourselves that gp34 and gp68 actually depend on one another to efficiently antagonize NK cell degranulation (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: gp34 consistently shows more rapid internalization compared to gp68.
source: While we find both, gp34 and gp68, able to internalize monomeric IgG as well as IC (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), gp34 consistently shows more rapid internalization compared to gp68 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exchange of the cytosolic domain of gp34 leads to strongly reduced internalization and subsequently to a reduction in FcγR antagonization.
source: Consequently exchange of the cytosolic domain of gp34 leads to strongly reduced internalization and subsequently to a reduction in FcγR antagonization (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The di-leucine motif found in gp34 is unique among other surface-resident glycoproteins expressed by HCMV and all other vFcγRs known in CMV family members including RhCMV and MCMV.
source: These findings highlight the di-leucine motif found in gp34 to be unique among other surface-resident glycoproteins expressed by HCMV and all other vFcγRs known in CMV family members including RhCMV and MCMV (Kolb et al., 2019; Thäle et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and citations to Kolb et al., 2019 and Thäle et al., 1994.

claim: gp34 is incorporated into the virion.
source: However, as we also find gp34 to be incorporated into the virion (Reinhard, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinhard, 2010.

claim: gp34 is not able to directly compete with host FcγRs for binding to IC on the plasma membrane when co-expressed with a target antigen.
source: This is remarkable given our data showing that gp34 binds to the hinge region of monomeric IgG, but implying that gp34 is not able to directly compete with host FcγRs for binding to IC on the plasma membrane when co-expressed with a target antigen.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: gp68 binding to the CH2–CH3 interface domain also occupies a region on Fcγ that includes residues involved in FcγRII and FcγRIII binding to Fcγ.
source: Conversely, gp68 binding to the CH2–CH3 interface domain also occupies a region on Fcγ that includes residues involved in FcγRII and FcγRIII binding to Fcγ (Shields et al., 2001; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shields et al., 2001 and Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: The blocking effect of gp68 is not total but more in line with the reported reduction of FcγRIII binding to IgG being approximately 40–70% when certain residues are manipulated.
source: The subordinate role of the above-mentioned residues on IgG regarding FcγRIII binding further ties into the observation that the blocking effect of gp68 is not total but more in line with the reported reduction of FcγRIII binding to IgG being approximately 40–70% when these residues are manipulated (Shields et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and a citation to Shields et al., 2001.

claim: Neither gp68 nor gp34 individually are able to efficiently antagonize FcγR activation by IgG-opsonized viral antigens in the physiological context of HCMV infection.
source: Taken together, we conclude that neither gp68 nor gp34 individually are able to efficiently antagonize FcγR activation by IgG-opsonized viral antigens in the physiological context of HCMV infection (Figure 2), that is, in the presence of non-immune IgG mitigating their inhibitory potential (Figure 6B and Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2, Figure 6B, and Figure 6C.

claim: gp68 functions to increase IC accessibility to gp34 leading to efficient internalization of IC, presumably by a repeating process of gp34 recycling.
source: Our data provide evidence that gp68 rather functions to increase IC accessibility to gp34 leading to efficient internalization of IC, presumably by a repeating process of gp34 recycling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The ectodomain of gp68 is sufficient to increase the antagonistic efficiency of gp34 regarding FcγR activation.
source: This is supported by our observation that the ectodomain of gp68 is sufficient to increase the antagonistic efficiency of gp34 regarding FcγR activation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: gp34 and gp68 are co-expressed at the cell surface throughout the protracted HCMV replication cycle and show simultaneous Fcγ binding.
source: Further, gp34 and gp68 are co-expressed at the cell surface throughout the protracted HCMV replication cycle and show simultaneous Fcγ binding (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: gp68 binding evolved to ensure a consistent and evolutionary less vulnerable way of shifting Fcγ accessibility in favor of gp34.
source: Our findings imply that gp68 binding, as it does not use the same region as host FcγRs, evolved to ensure a consistent and evolutionary less vulnerable way of shifting Fcγ accessibility in favor of gp34.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from experimental data.

claim: gp68 possesses a lower affinity to Fcγ when binding in a 2:1 ratio compared to host FcγRIIIA (KD1:470 nM and KD2:1.600 nM vs 700 nM).
source: The idea that gp68 has not evolved to directly compete with host receptors for IgG binding is also supported by the finding demonstrating gp68 to possess a lower affinity to Fcγ when binding in a 2:1 ratio compared to host FcγRIIIA (KD1:470 nM and KD2:1.600 nM vs 700 nM) (Li et al., 2007; Sprague et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2007 and Sprague et al., 2008.

claim: HCMV vFcγRs also antagonize activation of FcγRIIA (CD32) and FcγRI (CD64).
source: However, it is already known that HCMV vFcγRs also antagonize activation of FcγRIIA (CD32) and FcγRI (CD64) (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014b.

claim: HCMV vFcγRs antagonize activation of the only inhibitory FcγR, FcγRIIB.
source: and we also consistently observed antagonization of the only inhibitory FcγR, FcγRIIB (unpublished observation).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: gpRH05 antagonizes all canonical Rhesus FcγRs I, IIA, IIB, and III.
source: Similarly, we could recently show antagonization of all canonical Rhesus FcγRs I, IIA, IIB, and III by the RhCMV encoded vFcγR gpRH05 (RL11 gene family) (Kolb et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kolb et al., 2019.

claim: The HCMV RL11 gene family encodes additional vFcγRs: RL12 (gp95) and RL13 (gpRL13).
source: In support of this view, besides gp34 and gp68, the HCMV RL11 gene family encodes additional vFcγRs. RL12 (gp95) and RL13 (gpRL13) likely are part of a larger arsenal of antibody targeting immunoevasins (Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014a; Cortese et al., 2012).
